newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: OLYMPICS-MENEM CLAIMS CREDIT FOR BUENOS AIRES CHOICE.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-MENEM CLAIMS CREDIT FOR BUENOS AIRES CHOICE.

text.p: Argentines revelled on Friday after their capital made the shortlist to host the 2004 Summer Olympics and President Carlos Menem rushed to take credit and turn sports into politics during an election year.

"This happy development is an achievement of the national government which launched the project and endorsed it all along," Menem said after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) shortlisted Argentina's capital.
Menem, a keen golfer, soccer player and motor racing driver, faces mid-term legislative elections this October.

He told the state-run Telam news agency that the design of a 14-km by two-km "Olympic loop" stretching along the River Plate, where 90 percent of the events would take place, "elicited world-wide admiration".

The "Olympic loop" would run alongside downtown Buenos Aires and include the soccer stadiums of arch-rivals Boca Juniors and River Plate, the vast Luna Park stadium for boxing and other events, a horse track, a polo field, and the Buenos Aires lawn tennis club.

The IOC's selection committee named Athens, Buenos Aires, Cape Town, Rome and Stockholm from among 11 candidates after studying a detailed technical report of each bid. The final vote will be taken on September 5.
Istanbul, Lille, Rio de Janeiro, San Juan, Seville and St Petersburg failed to make the cut.
Sports Secretary Hugo Porta, a former rugby international, said Rio de Janeiro's failure to make the cut should ensure that neighbouring countries would back Buenos Aires's bid.
"We are now the only city from South America and we hope to have all South America behind us," he said from Lausanne, Switzerland, where he attended the IOC session.

In Brasilia, President Fernando Cardoso quickly closed ranks with Brazil's partners in the Mercosur trade bloc. While lamenting Rio's failure to make it, he said: "We are betting for Buenos Aires as representative of the Mercosur."
Immediately after the announcement dozens of teenage volunteers promoting the bid rushed into the streets chanting and handing out Olympic stickers.
"This fills all portenos (Buenos Aires dwellers) with pride," Mayor Fernando de la Rua said from Lausanne.
But he warned: "We have a lot of work to do until September."

This is the fifth time Buenos Aires has vied for the Olympic Games after failing in 1936, 1944, 1956, when it was runner-up, and 1968. Its selection offers South America the chance to stage the Olympics for the first time.
Buenos Aires, with relatively little street crime for a city of 12 million, is touting itself as a safe option.

On the downside, organisers admit that one of the biggest challenges for the city, which needs an estimated investment of $550 million, will be the need to boost hotel space by between 50 to 70 percent. And the IOC says its airports need major improvements.
